newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Jobless claims, 5-yr note sale.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Jobless claims, 5-yr note sale.

text.p: The weekly U.S. jobless claims report and the Treasury's monthly auction of five-year notes will likely highlight the U.S. government securities market trading session on Thursday, analysts said.

Jobless claims for the week ended May 24 are estimated to have totaled 321,000, barely changed from the 322,000 level of new claims a week earlier, according to economists polled by Reuters. The jobless data are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
On Thursday afternoon, the Treasury will sell $12.0 billion in five-year notes.
In late when-issued trade on Wednesday, the five-year notes to be sold in that auction offered yields of 6.645 percent.

The market will also get some privately collected economic data -- the May New York NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Managers) index at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT and the Conference Board's May Help Wanted Advertising Index at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. No forecast was available for the New York NAPM index which read 53.4 in April. Economists told Reuters they expect the Help-Wanted Advertising Index to stay level at 87 in May, unchanged from April.

Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds, said there would be a little more "apprehension" among bidders for the five-year notes after the lackluster Treasury sale of $16.5 billion in two-year notes on Wednesday.

"You were dealing with a stable Federal Reserve monetary policy for at least the next five weeks or so and an 80-bais-point spread over overnight money -- which was reasonably attractive," said Flanagan. "But the auction results were disappointing."
The two-year notes were sold at an average yield of 6.31 percent with yields tailing as high as 6.328 percent.
Flanagan also said that if the weekly jobless claims figures "show a decline of any note, that would be a problem for the market.

"The market is a little concerned about Fed policy being reactive rather than pro-active, about the Fed falling behind in its inflation fight," said Flanagan. "The steepening of the yield curve since they took no rate action last week (at the May 20 policy meeting) underscores that point."
The spread between yields on two- and 30-year maturities stood at 73 basis points, up from 66 basis points at the close of the week before the Fed meeting.
Greg Carr, market analyst at AG Edwards & Sons Inc, said the market was a little weaker "in the belly of the curve" in three- and five-year maturities.
"They're trying to cheapen it up and build in a concession for the five-year auction," he said. "The five-year auction will get done. It won't be a major stumbling block."
But Carr said the market's short-term bias is toward higher yields.
Analysts said the market would pay scant attention to the New York NAPM and to the Help Wanted Advertising Index.
"I don't think New York NAPM will have much of an impact at all," said Flanagan.
"Those reports make nice print but it's nothing that the traders will act on," said Carr. "The things they'll watch are jobless claims, the five-year auction and the dollar."
The dollar was firmer against the mark and yen in late New York dealings.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 94-31/32 on Wednesday, yielding 7.03 percent.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open at 5-1/2 percent to 5-9/16 percent on Thursday.
